Title: Impacts of Ethical Values on Sustainable Development in Nigeria: A Biblical Reflection on Matthew 5:3–10
Author: Selome Kuponu|Damilare Samuel ALAO
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: The pursuit of sustainable development has increasingly extended beyond economic growth to include ethical governance, social justice, environmental responsibility, and institutional accountability. Despite Nigeria’s abundant natural resources, youthful population, and strategic economic position in Africa, persistent corruption, weak public institutions, social inequality, environmental degradation, and declining public confidence continue to impede sustainable national development. While existing studies have largely interpreted these challenges through political, economic, or institutional frameworks, comparatively less attention has been given to the role of biblical ethics in shaping sustainable development discourse. This paper addresses that gap by examining how the ethical teachings of Jesus in Matthew 5:3–10, particularly the Beatitudes, provide a moral framework capable of strengthening responsible leadership, institutional integrity, and ethical citizenship within the Nigerian context. The study employs historical and sociological research methods complemented by theological-ethical analysis. Historical inquiry examines the evolution of ethical values within Nigeria’s socio-political development, while sociological analysis explores how family, education, religion, governance, and cultural institutions influence ethical behaviour in contemporary society. The Beatitudes are interpreted as an ethical paradigm through which issues of corruption, injustice, poor governance, and social fragmentation may be critically evaluated. The study argues that virtues such as humility, righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, and peacemaking possess enduring relevance for public administration and sustainable governance. It concludes that sustainable development cannot be sustained solely through economic reforms or institutional restructuring but requires deliberate moral formation among leaders and citizens alike. Accordingly, the paper recommends integrating biblical ethical principles with African communal values, civic education, and governance reforms to cultivate a development culture grounded in justice, accountability, compassion, and responsible stewardship.

Title: Implementation of al Maun Theology in Character Education in Muhammadiyah Schools
Author: Mudiana Ramadhani|Triono Ali Mustofa
Any location source: Proceeding ISETH (International Summit on Science Technology and Humanity)
Abstract: Character education in Indonesia is currently facing serious challenges in the form of administrative formalities and a dichotomy between ritual piety and social reality. The phenomenon of bullying, corruption, and loss of empathy is clear evidence of moral deterioration. This research aims to explore the implementation of Al-Ma'un Theology as the foundation of character education in Muhammadiyah schools in overcoming the moral crisis. The research method used is qualitative with a literature study approach. The results of the study show that Al-Ma'un Theology transforms the understanding of religion from texts to social actions through three main pillars: the cultivation of the character of generosity, the internalization of social piety, and the use of the Ismuba curriculum as an instrument of value. This implementation succeeded in synergizing individual piety with public concern, where students were educated to have empathy for the poor through real philanthropic practices. In the digital era, Al-Ma'un values are relevant as a fortress of ethics and digital moral literacy. This research confirms that Al Ma'un-based character education creates 'organic intellectuals' who are not only personally pious, but also socially progressive, so as to be able to answer global humanitarian challenges and the nation's moral crisis.

Title: Governance Deficits and Reform Trajectories in Bangladesh: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Public Administration Effectiveness
Author: Mohammad Rafiqul Islam|Sharmin Akhter|Tanvir Ahmed Chowdhury
Any location source: Administrative Science and Policy Analysis
Abstract: Bangladesh has undergone substantial administrative restructuring since its independence in 1971, yet systemic governance deficits persist across its bureaucratic apparatus. Most existing evaluations, however, are either macro-institutional overviews or narrow, single-sector assessments, and rarely combine citizen-level survey evidence, elite qualitative testimony, and formal statistical modelling of satisfaction predictors within one design. This study investigates the effectiveness of public administration in Bangladesh through an explanatory sequential mixed-methods framework, combining a structured questionnaire survey of 1,200 citizens across all eight administrative divisions with 480 key informant interviews drawn from civil servants, policy experts, and civil society representatives. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and ordinal logistic regression, with full coefficient, odds-ratio, and goodness-of-fit reporting, while qualitative findings were processed through thematic analysis and integrated with quantitative results via a joint display. Results indicate that e-governance adoption has improved service delivery indices particularly in urban areas, but rural-urban disparities remain pronounced (rural odds of satisfaction 56% lower than urban, OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.35, 0.56]). Anti-corruption initiatives show partial gains, with the Control of Corruption indicator improving from −0.99 in 2019 to −0.92 in 2022 on the World Governance Indicators scale, despite comparatively high implementation ratings for several reforms, a decoupling this study examines critically. Citizen satisfaction with public service quality remains low (49.2% dissatisfied overall), driven primarily by bureaucratic delays, bribery, and inadequate decentralisation. Five primary governance challenges are identified, alongside stakeholder-endorsed reform strategies centred on RTI strengthening, digital infrastructure expansion, and civil service ethics reform, which are translated into a prioritised implementation agenda naming responsible institutions and anticipated barriers. The findings contribute to the comparative public administration literature on South Asian and lower-middle-income developing states and offer evidence-based policy recommendations for the Government of Bangladesh.

Title: Analisis Yuridis Terhadap Tindak Pidana Penyalahgunaan Wewenang oleh Anggota DPRD Dalam Pengawasan Pelaksanaan Peraturan Daerah (Studi Pada Kantor DPRD Labuhan Batu)
Author: Sahbudi Sahbudi|Akiruddin Ahmad|Mahmuddin Hasibuan
Any location source: Journal of Education Humaniora and Social Sciences (JEHSS)
Abstract: This study aims to analyze the abuse of authority by members of the Regional House of Representatives (DPRD) in exercising the supervisory function over Regional Regulations in Labuhanbatu Regency from the perspective of administrative law. The study focuses on the legal framework governing DPRD authority, forms of misuse of authority in the implementation of supervisory functions, and mechanisms of accountability and prevention. This research employs an empirical legal research method using statutory and conceptual approaches. Data were obtained through interviews with relevant parties within the Labuhanbatu DPRD and document analysis of legal regulations and supporting documents. The results show that DPRD supervisory authority is legally regulated through the Regional Government Law, Government Administration Law, the Law on the People's Consultative Assembly, House of Representatives, Regional Representative Council, and Regional House of Representatives (MD3 Law), as well as regulations on corruption eradication. However, the implementation of supervision still faces gaps between legal norms and practices, particularly regarding the potential politicization of supervisory functions, conflicts of interest in budgeting processes, lack of objectivity in oversight, and inadequate control over the implementation of DPRD members’ constituency aspiration programs. Prevention of authority abuse is carried out through strengthening the DPRD Ethics Council, improving members’ capacity, implementing technology-based transparency, and increasing public participation. This study confirms that the effectiveness of DPRD supervision is influenced not only by regulations but also by institutional integrity, legislative capacity, and public accountability mechanisms.

Title: Behavioural Economics and King V: Understanding the Human Side of Corporate Governance
Author: Dumisani Pamba
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: This paper examines South Africa’s new King V governance framework through the lens of behavioural economics. The central argument is that many corporate governance failures do not arise because boards lack formal rules; they arise because real people misperceive incentives, defer to authority, overestimate their own judgement, silence dissent, rationalise doubtful conduct and prioritise short-term gain over long-term value. Behavioural economics therefore helps to explain why formally compliant organisations can still fail ethically, strategically and institutionally. King V, released on 31 October 2025 and effective for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026, responds to a changed governance environment in South Africa. It simplifies the code, standardises disclosure and sharpens guidance on ethics, sustainability, independence, committee composition, remuneration, and the governance of data, information, technology and artificial intelligence. Read behaviourally, King V recognises that governance quality depends on how people actually decide, challenge, escalate concerns and justify outcomes in practice (IoDSA, 2025). The South African evidence is compelling. Transparency International reports a 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index score of 41/100 for South Africa, with 64% of respondents believing corruption increased in the previous 12 months and 18% of public service users reporting bribe payment. Auditor-General South Africa reports continued fruitless and wasteful expenditure, unauthorised expenditure, deficits and governance failures across public institutions. Corporate scandals such as Steinhoff and Tongaat Hulett, together with the state capture findings concerning Eskom and Transnet, demonstrate the practical consequences of authority bias, incentive distortion, cultural silence and weak challenge mechanisms. The paper concludes that South African organisations should implement King V as a behavioural operating system rather than a disclosure checklist. That means redesigning board information flows, strengthening committee independence, aligning remuneration with long-term value, institutionalising devil’s-advocate challenge, governing AI with human accountability, and building speak-up cultures that reward evidence-based dissent. These changes are especially important in forensic governance, risk management and institutional performance because they target the human conditions that allow control failures to persist.

Read behaviourally, King V recognises that governance quality depends on how people actually decide, challenge, escalate concerns and justify outcomes in practice (IoDSA, 2025). The South African evidence is compelling. Transparency International reports a 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index score of 41/100 for South Africa, with 64% of respondents believing corruption increased in the previous 12 months and 18% of public service users reporting bribe payment. Auditor-General South Africa reports continued fruitless and wasteful expenditure, unauthorised expenditure, deficits and governance failures across public institutions. Corporate scandals such as Steinhoff and Tongaat Hulett, together with the state capture findings concerning Eskom and Transnet, demonstrate the practical consequences of authority bias, incentive distortion, cultural silence and weak challenge mechanisms. The paper concludes that South African organisations should implement King V as a behavioural operating system rather than a disclosure checklist. That means redesigning board information flows, strengthening committee independence, aligning remuneration with long-term value, institutionalising devil’s-advocate challenge, governing AI with human accountability, and building speak-up cultures that reward evidence-based dissent. These changes are especially important in forensic governance, risk management and institutional performance because they target the human conditions that allow control failures to persist.

Title: Reformulation of Criminal Law Policy and Islamic Law Perspective in Addressing Misuse of Regional Assets as an Effort to Prevent State Losses
Author: Malikal Mulki
Any location source: Jurnal Iman dan Spiritualitas
Abstract: This study aims to analyze criminal law policies regarding the misuse of Regional Government Property (Barang Milik Daerah/BMD) and to reconstruct a preventive framework against state financial losses through positive law and Islamic law perspectives. The key concepts and definitions utilized include criminal law policy, misuse of regional assets, state financial losses, asset governance, and maqāṣid al-sharīʿah principles (ḥifẓ al-māl and the prohibition of ghulūl). A normative-juridical research method was employed, incorporating statutory, conceptual, comparative, and Islamic legal approaches supported by primary legal materials and contemporary scholarly literature. The object and scope of the research focus on the national regulatory architecture of regional asset management—including laws on state finance and treasury, government regulations, and home affairs ministerial regulations—synchronized with anti-corruption enforcement and public governance ethics. The main findings indicate that foundational weaknesses stem from fragmented asset databases, weak internal controls, and a lack of integration between preventive controls and enforcement, resulting in the delayed detection of asset misappropriation until large-scale fiscal losses materialize. The challenges or constraints of the research involve bureaucratic regulatory dynamics that lag behind modern risk mitigation requirements and the complexity of proving non-cash economic losses. Recommendations and practical implications highlight the necessity of establishing interoperable digital asset information systems, risk-based internal auditing, standardized commercial utilization contracts, and integrated asset recovery mechanisms.

Title: Staff Discipline and Organizational Performance in Rivers State Post Primary School Board, 2015-2025
Author: Fredrick Nwojie
Any location source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
Abstract: Staff discipline has been identified as a critical factor influencing the performance of public educational institutions, with indiscipline manifested through absenteeism, lateness, truancy, poor work attitude, corruption, and unprofessional conduct significantly undermining service delivery and educational outcomes. This study examined the relationship between Staff discipline and organizational performance in the Rivers State Post Primary Schools Board between 2015 and 2025. this study was instituted to achieve 1 objective, which give rise to 1 research questions and was guided by 1 null hypotheses. The study adopted Control Theory as the theoretical foundation to discern how staff discipline influences organizational performance in Rivers State schools. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, using structured questionnaire administered to 378 purposively selected respondents, including teachers, school administrators, and supervisory staff. Secondary data were sourced from official records, policy documents, and scholarly publications to provide contextual and historical perspectives on staff discipline and organizational performance. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including means, percentages, and standard deviations, while Pearson Product Moment Correlation (PPMC) was applied to test relationships between variables at a 0.05 significance level. Findings revealed that disciplined staffers significantly improved organizational performance by enhancing punctuality, accountability, adherence to rules, and overall teaching quality. Conversely, teacher indiscipline negatively affected instructional time, disrupted school schedules, reduced student learning outcomes, and diminished institutional efficiency. The study also found that work ethics including commitment, diligence, and responsibility positively influenced staff performance and productivity. Major challenges affecting discipline included weak supervision, inadequate enforcement of rules, lack of motivation, political interference, and unfavorable working conditions. The study concluded that staff discipline is fundamental to the effective functioning of public schools and that strengthening disciplinary mechanisms, promoting strong work ethics, and improving institutional support systems are essential for enhancing productivity, service delivery, and educational outcomes. The study recommends among others that; a transparent and fair disciplinary system should be established by the government to ensure that disciplinary measures are consistently applied to erring staffers without bias or political interference.

Title: La crueldad y los límites de la fuerza: Valerio Máximo y la ética del mando militar
Author: Andrés Miguel Cosialls Ubach
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: LEGAL REVIEW Cosialls Ubach, Andrés Miguel. “La crueldad y los límites de la fuerza: Valerio Máximo y la ética del mando militar.” Boletín CODESEL, vol. 2, no. 10, August 2026, ISSN-e: 3045-7750. Review The ethical limits governing the exercise of military force are often examined through contemporary legal doctrine, professional military ethics or the law of armed conflict. Yet the problem itself is considerably older. Classical authors already understood that the corruption of power does not arise only from injustice or ambition, but also from the manner in which force is exercised. In this concise and intellectually suggestive article, Andrés Miguel Cosialls Ubach turns to Valerius Maximus and the opening of the chapter De crudelitate in the Facta et dicta memorabilia to explore the ethical meaning of cruelty and its relationship with military command. The central argument is compelling: cruelty is not simply excessive violence, but a corruption of authority produced when force ceases to be governed by reason, duty and measure. One of the article’s principal strengths lies in the author’s decision to analyse cruelty not primarily through the acts it produces but through the character of the person who exercises it. Valerius Maximus describes cruelty through the expressions horridus habitus, truculenta species, violenti spiritus and vox terribilis. Cosialls Ubach interprets these formulations as indicating a progressive transformation of the agent: cruelty ceases to be an isolated action and becomes a stable disposition, a way of exercising power and ultimately a mode of being. This distinction is especially relevant to military ethics. The ethical problem does not arise only when a commander orders an objectively unlawful or unnecessary act. It also emerges when violence becomes habitual, when intimidation becomes the normal language of authority, and when the use of force begins to shape the commander’s character. The article thus moves beyond an exclusively external theory of restraint and towards an internal ethics of command. Particularly effective is the analysis of the expression minis et cruentis imperiis referta—filled with threats and bloody commands. Cosialls Ubach correctly focuses on the importance of the word imperia. Valerius Maximus is not merely condemning violent episodes; he is describing a form of command. Cruelty corrupts authority because force ceases to remain subordinate to a legitimate purpose and begins to function as its own justification. This insight allows the author to formulate one of the article’s central distinctions: severity may be necessary in military life, whereas cruelty is always a deviation from the proper exercise of force. Combat can require decisions of extraordinary hardness. Military ethics therefore cannot be reduced to an ideal of gentleness or avoidance of force. The decisive criterion lies elsewhere: whether force remains subordinated to duty, necessity and measure. The article’s treatment of cui silentium donare crementum est adicere is particularly powerful. Cosialls Ubach translates the phrase as the idea that remaining silent before cruelty is to contribute to its growth. Valerius Maximus is thus interpreted as recognising the expansive character of unrestrained violence: cruelty does not naturally moderate itself. Silence, indifference and passivity can therefore become forms of complicity because they remove the external resistance necessary to stop its expansion. This proposition has obvious relevance for contemporary military institutions. The prevention of abuse depends not only upon rules addressed to those who directly employ force but also upon institutional cultures capable of identifying, rejecting and reporting cruelty. A command structure in which subordinates, colleagues or superiors remain silent before abusive conduct risks allowing exceptional behaviour to become normalised. The following question—quem modum sibi ipsa statuet?, “what limit will it impose upon itself?”—provides the philosophical centre of the article. The answer is implicit: none. Cruelty is defined precisely by the absence of self-limitation. The deeper danger of cruelty therefore lies not only in the immediate harm it inflicts, but in the destruction of the very principle by which force can be contained. Cosialls Ubach uses this classical insight to illuminate a fundamental principle of military command. The possession of power does not legitimise its unrestricted use. On the contrary, genuine command becomes visible precisely where an actor possesses the capacity to exceed limits but deliberately remains within them. Self-restraint is therefore not weakness; it is one of the clearest manifestations of disciplined authority. The discussion of cum penes illam sit timeri, penes nos sit odisse adds another important normative dimension. Cosialls Ubach observes that penes denotes what lies within someone’s power or control. Valerius Maximus thus opposes two forms of power: cruelty possesses the capacity to produce fear, while the political community retains the moral power—and duty—to reject it. The formulation makes a crucial distinction between suffering cruelty and legitimising it. Fear may be unavoidable, but acceptance is not. This opposition between fear and legitimacy is particularly relevant to armed forces. Military effectiveness may involve the capacity to inspire fear in an adversary, yet that capacity cannot become the normative foundation of command itself. Authority grounded solely in intimidation ceases to be disciplined authority and approaches the condition described by Valerius Maximus as cruelty. The article’s final reflections develop this point with considerable force. The excellence of the soldier does not consist in demonstrating the maximum extent to which force can be employed. It consists in knowing the point beyond which force must never pass. The ethical quality of command is therefore measured by self-mastery under conditions of power. This formulation has a strong affinity with contemporary military professionalism. Armed forces entrust commanders with extraordinary powers precisely because they are expected to exercise them under legal, ethical and institutional constraints. Discipline is therefore not merely obedience to orders; it also involves control over the instruments of violence. One of the study’s most valuable contributions is its implicit distinction between force and cruelty. Force may remain lawful, necessary and proportionate. Cruelty begins when violence becomes detached from a legitimate objective and acquires an autonomous logic. This distinction resonates strongly with contemporary principles governing the conduct of hostilities, even though the article proceeds primarily through philosophical rather than doctrinal legal analysis. The study also invites comparison with the modern prohibition of unnecessary suffering and with the broader humanitarian logic underlying International Humanitarian Law. Contemporary law seeks to regulate not only whether force may be used, but how it may be used. The principle that military necessity does not authorise unlimited violence reflects, in juridical form, the same underlying idea found in Valerius Maximus: force must remain governed by measure. The article’s brevity is itself one of its strengths. Rather than attempting a general theory of military ethics, Cosialls Ubach concentrates on a very short classical passage and extracts from it a coherent set of principles concerning character, authority, restraint, institutional responsibility and legitimacy. The result demonstrates the continuing analytical value of classical sources for contemporary military thought. The visual design of the page reinforces this compact philosophical structure. The highlighted statement—“La primera victoria del militar no consiste en vencer al enemigo, sino en impedir que el ejercicio de la fuerza termine por vencer su propia humanidad”—functions almost as a synthesis of the article’s argument. Military victory deprived of moral self-command may amount to a deeper defeat of the person exercising force. Methodologically, the study combines close textual interpretation with contemporary military philosophy. Latin terminology is not employed decoratively; each expression is examined for the conceptual implications it carries. This allows the article to show how a seemingly rhetorical passage in Valerius Maximus contains a sophisticated account of the psychology and ethics of power. From a leadership perspective, the article is particularly relevant because it identifies cruelty as a failure of command before it becomes merely a failure of conduct. A commander dominated by violence has already lost part of the internal discipline required to exercise authority legitimately. Ethical leadership therefore demands not only knowledge of rules but also the cultivation of character. This approach also helps explain why institutional safeguards are necessary. Because cruelty does not naturally impose limits upon itself, military organisations require external limits: law, doctrine, command responsibility, supervision, reporting mechanisms and professional education. The classical insight and the modern institutional framework converge on the same conclusion—the use of force must never depend exclusively upon the self-restraint of the person who possesses it. There is also a deeper political dimension. When cruelty becomes embedded in systems of command, the damage extends beyond individual victims. It corrodes the legitimacy of the institution exercising force and alters the relationship between authority and the community it serves. The corruption described by Valerius Maximus is therefore simultaneously moral, military and political. Overall, this article constitutes a concise but original contribution to military ethics and the philosophy of command. Andrés Miguel Cosialls Ubach demonstrates t

Title: GRATIFIKASI SEBAGAI PELANGGARAN ETIK DI BURSA EFEK INDONESIA
Author: Innayati Diah Sukmaningtias|Agung Firman Sampurna
Any location source: E-Jurnal Manajemen Universitas Udayana
Abstract: Integritas sektor jasa keuangan di Indonesia yang tercermin dari hasil Survei Penilaian Integritas (SPI) tahun 2025 yang menempatkan Indonesia dalam kategori “Rentan Korupsi”. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis urgensi pencegahan gratifikasi sebagai bentuk pelanggaran etik di Bursa Efek Indonesia (BEI). Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif deskriptif, fenomena gratifikasi melalui studi literatur dan analisis data sekunder dari laporan Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi (KPK) periode 2021-2025. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa meskipun integritas lembaga secara agregat dinilai terjaga, terjadi penurunan signifikan pada aspek penilaian ahli (Indeks Eksper) yang berkaitan dengan potensi suap, konflik kepentingan, dan intervensi pihak luar. Analisis menggunakan kerangka Fraud Diamond Theory mengungkapkan bahwa pelanggaran di BEI dipicu oleh adanya tekanan target kuantitas emiten, celah kesempatan dalam sistem pengawasan, rasionalisasi tindakan sebagai "jasa teknis", serta kapabilitas individu dalam memanfaatkan jabatan. Dampak dari praktik ini bukan sekadar masalah administratif, melainkan mencederai kepercayaan publik dan menurunkan kualitas emiten di pasar modal. Sebagai langkah mitigasi, penelitian ini menegaskan pentingnya penguatan kode etik organisasi yang terintegrasi dan sinergi pengawasan lintas lembaga untuk menutup celah praktik tidak etis yang dapat merusak ekosistem investasi nasional. The integrity of the financial services sector in Indonesia is reflected in the results of the 2025 Integrity Assessment Survey (SPI) which places Indonesia in the category of "Vulnerable to Corruption". This study aims to analyze the urgency of gratuity prevention as a form of ethical violation on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX). The research uses a descriptive qualitative approach, the phenomenon of gratuities through literature studies and secondary data analysis from the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) report for the 2021-2025 period. The results showed that although the integrity of the institution was assessed as aggregate maintained, there was a significant decrease in the aspect of expert assessment (Expert Index) related to potential bribery, conflicts of interest, and external intervention. Analysis using the Fraud Diamond Theory framework revealed that violations on the IDX were triggered by the pressure of issuer quantity targets, opportunities gaps in the supervisory system, rationalization of actions as "technical services", and individual capabilities in utilizing positions. The impact of this practice is not just an administrative problem, but it hurts public trust and lowers the quality of issuers in the capital market. As a mitigation measure, this study emphasizes the importance of strengthening an integrated organizational code of ethics and cross-agency supervision synergy to close the loopholes of unethical practices that can damage the national investment ecosystem.

Title: Governance and Infrastructural Development in Benue State
Author: Twar Sylvester Orkume
Any location source: JOURNAL OF POLITICAL SCIENCE AND LEADERSHIP RESEARCH
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between governance and infrastructural development in Benue State, Nigeria, with the objective of assessing how governance quality, institutional actions, and policy processes influence the pace and quality of infrastructure delivery. It interrogates why Benue State, despite its abundant human and natural resources, continues to experience infrastructural decay, unemployment, and poverty. Anchored on elite theory, the paper adopts a conceptual and theoretical approach to analyse how governance practices, policy priorities, and institutional structures shape development outcomes. The study posits that infrastructural progress is largely determined by a small ruling class that controls political and economic power within governance systems. Drawing from the works of Pareto (1935) and Mosca (1939), it argues that governance elites governors, policymakers, and senior bureaucrats exercise disproportionate influence over decision-making and resource allocation. The successes and failures of infrastructural development in Benue State are therefore linked to the capacity, ethics, and orientation of governance institutions and actors. Findings reveal that Nigeria’s colonial legacy fostered a self-serving governance culture oriented toward personal enrichment rather than public service. This pattern persists in Benue State, resulting in weak institutions, corruption, poor policy continuity, and abandoned projects. Nonetheless, recent governance efforts, such as Governor Alia’s declaration of an infrastructural emergency and the allocation of ₦149.5 billion to road and water projects, demonstrate renewed commitment to development. The study concludes that governance and infrastructure are deeply interconnected. Infrastructural progress depends less on resource availability and more on political will, accountability, inclusivity, and institutional effectiveness. Sustainable infrastructural growth in Benue State requires good governance, institutional continuity, transparency, and citizen participation to ensure that public authority transcends elite self-interest and promotes collective welfare.

Title: State-Building and Governance in the Speeches and Discourses of His Eminence Sayyid Ammar al-Hakim (Volume I: 2011 - 2012 - 2013).
Author: Sayyid Ammar Alhakeem
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: This book presents a comprehensive strategic vision and programmatic framework formulated by Sayyid Ammar al-Hakim to rebuild the Iraqi state and its institutions during a critical transitional phase marked by two pivotal turning points: the fall of tyranny and the end of foreign presence. This vision represents the culmination of daily engagement and interaction with Iraqi reality at both the popular and governmental levels. The book is distinguished by its constructive, critical approach to administrative flaws and corruption, steering clear of abstract theorizing and classical political thought. Its thesis is built upon the interconnectedness of three structural pillars: first, the pillar of science and knowledge to ensure sustainable development; second, the pillar of ethics and Islamic values as a civilized foundation to resolve the debate between the secular and the religious; and third, the pillar of strategic planning to effectively leverage Iraq’s geographical, economic, and human assets. The book is structured into three main chapters alongside an analytical conclusion evaluating his political discourse. The first chapter reviews detailed developmental plans and strategic initiatives for the revitalization of major provinces (such as "Basra as Iraq’s Economic Capital," "Dhi Qar as the Gateway to the South," "Najaf as Iraq's Scientific Capital," as well as development initiatives for Maysan, Babylon, Wasit, Al-Muthanna, Karbala, Al-Diwaniyah, and Baghdad) aimed at achieving self-sufficiency and economic integration. The second chapter focuses on social development, particularly child welfare through a national initiative to establish an independent child support fund, alongside empowering women and advancing the education sector. The third chapter engages academic and economic spheres to offer realistic solutions for transitioning toward comprehensive renaissance, national security, and sovereignty. Ultimately, the book serves as a rational, dialogue-driven guide for managing complexity and establishing the foundations of a just and contemporary civil state.

Title: Entrepreneurial Avowal: Confession as Symbolic Capital and Moral Revaluation in Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger
Author: Surbhi Goswami|Dr Reenu
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: Aravind Adiga’s The White Tiger is frequently discussed as a satire of caste hierarchy, corruption, and the violent promise of social mobility in post-liberalisation India. This article relocates the centre of analysis from Balram Halwai’s ambition to the form through which he makes his rise intelligible: the seven nights of letters addressed to the Chinese Premier. It argues that Balram’s narration is an entrepreneurial avowal - a confession that acknowledges wrongdoing while refusing repentance and institutional judgement. Bringing Michel Foucault’s account of avowal into conversation with neoliberal governmentality, Ulrich Bröckling’s entrepreneurial self, Wendy Brown’s economisation of political and moral life, Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of symbolic capital, and James Phelan’s narrative ethics, the article develops the concept of confession as symbolic conversion. Balram turns stolen money into economic capital, knowledge acquired in servitude into cultural competence, a fugitive identity into an entrepreneurial brand, and murder into a founding story of risk and innovation. Close readings of the absent addressee, the ‘original listener,’ the Rooster Coop, the murder of Ashok, the name Ashok Sharma, and the Bangalore taxi business show that the confession continues the work of self-making after the crime. Yet Adiga’s irony prevents Balram’s moral vocabulary from becoming the novel’s final judgement. The narrative grants him voice without granting innocence, and mobility without equating it with emancipation. The article therefore, distinguishes moral relativism from moral revaluation: Balram does not prove that moral standards disappear; he strategically reranks loyalty, betrayal, violence, and responsibility according to mobility, risk, and return. The White Tiger finally exposes the narrative labour through which neoliberal success converts structural injury into personal legitimacy, while leaving its human costs outside the entrepreneur’s account.

The third chapter engages academic and economic spheres to offer realistic solutions for transitioning toward comprehensive renaissance, national security, and sovereignty. Ultimately, the book serves as a rational, dialogue-driven guide for managing complexity and establishing the foundations of a just and contemporary civil state.

Title: Reconstructing the PAI-STEAM Curriculum Based on Maqāshid Al-Sharīʿa in Civil Engineering Programs at Public Universities
Author: Rahmadi Agus Setiawan
Any location source: At Turots Jurnal Pendidikan Islam
Abstract: The construction sector in Indonesia faces an ethical crisis spanning structural failures that endanger life, pervasive corruption, and ecological degradation, problems that are fundamentally moral rather than merely technical. Islamic Religious Education (PAI) in public universities is institutionally positioned to address this crisis, yet in engineering faculties it remains normative-textual and epistemologically isolated from students' technical disciplines. This study aims to reconstruct an integrated PAI-STEAM curriculum for civil engineering programs by operationalizing the maqāshid al-sharīʿa as an ethics of infrastructure engineering aligned with global accreditation standards. Employing qualitative library research with a philosophical-hermeneutic approach, the study analyzes Islamic juridical sources and engineering-accreditation documents through transdisciplinary content analysis and creative synthesis. The study yields three principal results. First, integration requires dissolving the dichotomy of knowledge at the epistemological level, repositioning engineering laws as sunnat Allāh and the STEAM "Arts" component as an axiological gateway for ethical values. Second, the five maqāshid pillars (hifdz al-nafs, hifdz al-bīʾah, hifdz al-māl, hifdz al-ʿaql, and hifdz al-dīn) map onto assessable engineering domains that correspond directly to IABEE accreditation criteria, consolidated in a Complementarity Matrix. Third, an Integrated Project-Based Learning model (IPBL-OBE), anchored in a Green Eco-Mosque capstone project, translates these correspondences into measurable graduate outcomes. The study contributes a novel epistemological framework and a ready curriculum template, repositioning PAI from an accreditation-neutral formality into a substantive accreditation asset. The proposed framework is intended to serve as a practical reference for curriculum developers, PAI lecturers, and engineering faculty seeking to design accreditation-aligned, values-based learning experiences, while acknowledging that its pedagogical claims await empirical validation.

Title: A DESCRIPTIVE ETHICAL STUDY OF AFRICAN CONCEPT OF LAW AND PUBLIC MORALITY
Author: Etaoghene Paul Polo|Ayodeji Felix SOYEMI
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: This article provides a descriptive ethical study of the African concept of law and public morality. Descriptive ethics is concerned with describing and explaining the moral beliefs and practices that actually exist in a society, rather than prescribing what ought to be. The study, therefore, seeks to describe how law and public morality are understood and practised in the African traditional setting. The methodology adopted for this study is qualitative and library-based. It relies on a critical analysis of relevant literature in African philosophy, anthropology, sociology and legal studies. It also draws on ethnographic accounts of traditional African societies and the works of leading African philosophers. The approach is interpretive and descriptive. The findings of the study show that in the African worldview, law and public morality are not strictly separated. Both have their roots in the community and in shared spiritual beliefs. African law is mainly customary, unwritten and restorative in nature. Its main purpose is not to punish the offender but to restore harmony, peace and balance in the community. Public morality in Africa is communal, and it is based on values such as respect for elders, honesty, hospitality, hard work, sanctity of life and solidarity. An individual is seen as moral only to the extent that he or she contributes to the wellbeing of the community. This is well expressed in the famous saying, I am because we are. The study also finds that taboos, proverbs, folktales and ancestral sanctions play a central role in sustaining law and public morality. The study recommends that modern African legal systems should pay more attention to restorative justice and community based dispute resolution mechanisms that are rooted in African culture. It also recommends that African public morality should be taught in schools and promoted through community institutions to address contemporary moral challenges such as corruption, individualism and loss of community spirit. There is a need to create a dialogue between modern state law and African customary law so that both can work together for justice and social order.

Title: Entrepreneurial Avowal: Confession as Symbolic Capital and Moral Revaluation in Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger
Author: Surbhi Goswami|Dr Reenu
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: Aravind Adiga’s The White Tiger is frequently discussed as a satire of caste hierarchy, corruption, and the violent promise of social mobility in post-liberalisation India. This article relocates the centre of analysis from Balram Halwai’s ambition to the form through which he makes his rise intelligible: the seven nights of letters addressed to the Chinese Premier. It argues that Balram’s narration is an entrepreneurial avowal - a confession that acknowledges wrongdoing while refusing repentance and institutional judgement. Bringing Michel Foucault’s account of avowal into conversation with neoliberal governmentality, Ulrich Bröckling’s entrepreneurial self, Wendy Brown’s economisation of political and moral life, Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of symbolic capital, and James Phelan’s narrative ethics, the article develops the concept of confession as symbolic conversion. Balram turns stolen money into economic capital, knowledge acquired in servitude into cultural competence, a fugitive identity into an entrepreneurial brand, and murder into a founding story of risk and innovation. Close readings of the absent addressee, the ‘original listener,’ the Rooster Coop, the murder of Ashok, the name Ashok Sharma, and the Bangalore taxi business show that the confession continues the work of self-making after the crime. Yet Adiga’s irony prevents Balram’s moral vocabulary from becoming the novel’s final judgement. The narrative grants him voice without granting innocence, and mobility without equating it with emancipation. The article therefore, distinguishes moral relativism from moral revaluation: Balram does not prove that moral standards disappear; he strategically reranks loyalty, betrayal, violence, and responsibility according to mobility, risk, and return. The White Tiger finally exposes the narrative labour through which neoliberal success converts structural injury into personal legitimacy, while leaving its human costs outside the entrepreneur’s account.

Title: Rediscovering Strategic Leadership: What Ancient Indian Statecraft Teaches Modern Executives and Policymakers
Author: P. S. Aithal|Ramanathan Srinivasan
Any location source: Poornaprajna International Journal of Philosophy & Languages (PIJPL)|Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)|Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: Purpose: The contemporary global leadership crisis — characterised by endemic institutional corruption, short-term decision-making driven by quarterly earnings cycles, the collapse of trust between organisations and their stakeholders, and the widespread failure of leaders under pressure — has generated a searching re-examination of whether the foundational assumptions of modern Western management theory are adequate for the leadership challenges of the twenty-first century. This deep-study research paper argues that the ancient Indian tradition of statecraft offers a remarkably sophisticated, philosophically coherent, and practically tested alternative framework for understanding and developing leadership — one that addresses precisely those dimensions of leadership that modern theory consistently neglects: inner character formation, philosophical training as a prerequisite for strategic thinking, the integration of ethics and governance, the practice of non-attached action, and the orientation of all leadership activity toward the welfare of those being led. Methodology: In this paper, the exploratory qualitative research method is used. The relevant information is collected using keyword-based search in Google search engine, Google Scholar search engine, and AI-driven GPTs. This information is analysed and interpreted as per the objectives of the paper. Analysis/ Results: Drawing upon the four principal classical sources of ancient Indian leadership thought — Kautilya's Arthashastra, the Bhagavad Gita, Thiruvalluvar's Thirukkural, and Kamandaka's Nitisara — alongside secondary sources from the Mahabharata, Ramayana, and Panchatantra, this paper systematically analyses six foundational dimensions of ancient Indian leadership theory: the concept of the Raja-rishi or sage-king as the ideal leader; the conquest of the Shadripus (six internal enemies) as the prerequisite for effective leadership; the four-subject educational curriculum (Anvikshiki, Trayi, Varta, Dandaniti) prescribed for aspiring leaders; the art of counsel, decision-making, and task completion; the communication principles of the Thirukkural; and the ethical governance framework of Rajadharma and Yogakshema. Each dimension is examined both in its classical historical context and in its contemporary management application, with specific attention to what modern leadership theory and practice miss by ignoring these ancient sources. Originality/ Values: The paper concludes that ancient Indian statecraft offers not a romanticised alternative to modern management theory but a deeper and more demanding foundation for it — one that begins where modern theory rarely begins, with the leader's own inner life, and ends where modern theory rarely arrives, with the genuinely selfless orientation of leadership toward collective welfare. Type of Paper: Exploratory Research.

Title: OSINT Dossier: Evidence of Systemic Financial Misconduct at the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR
Author: Marie-Soleil Seshat Landry (Marie Landry Spy Shop)
Any location source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: ⚡ TL;DR: This dossier aggregates four decades of financial records, court convictions, and whistleblower reports to demonstrate that the Vatican Bank's structural design fosters systemic financial opacity and conflicts of interest. Abstract: This dossier compiles publicly available evidence documenting a pattern of systemic financial misconduct at the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), spanning four decades, involving convicted high-ranking Vatican officials, hundreds of suspicious financial transactions, and credible whistleblower allegations of deliberate financial manipulation. The evidence originates from official Vatican court documents, international news organizations, regulatory body reports, and statements from direct witnesses with institutional access. Key Takeaways & Executive Highlights The Vatican Bank maintains an opaque financial structure with no requirement for beneficial ownership disclosure, masking the ultimate controllers of its €6 billion portfolio. A statistically significant 78% of all Vatican-linked Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) are tied directly to the IOR, signaling potential structural flaws in compliance. The Pope holds absolute, unchecked authority over IOR assets, acting simultaneously as owner, regulator, and final arbiter in misconduct cases. Recent court rulings (2026) have highlighted significant procedural irregularities in the Vatican's justice system, complicating the finality of high-profile financial crime convictions. Novelties & Core Innovations Synthesizes disparate evidence across 40 years to demonstrate a recurring historical pattern rather than isolated incidents. Quantifies the concentration of financial risk by linking 78% of systemic suspicious activity to the IOR. Provides a critical structural analysis of the 'vow of poverty' versus absolute institutional financial control. Maps the chain of command from the Vatican Secretariat to the Pope to illustrate how sovereign status prevents external regulatory oversight. Documents the technical allegations regarding IBAN manipulation (the 'skeleton key' hypothesis) within the SWIFT network. Analyzes the impact of the 2026 Vatican appellate court's challenge to papal procedural decrees. Summary & Key Contributions This investigative report provides a comprehensive examination of the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), commonly known as the Vatican Bank, focusing on a recurring pattern of financial malfeasance. By analyzing official Vatican criminal tribunal records alongside international financial reports, the dossier outlines specific criminal schemes, including the embezzlement of millions of euros by former IOR president Angelo Caloia and the complex real estate fraud involving Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu. The analysis emphasizes the intersection of institutional sovereign status and weak oversight mechanisms. The report critically evaluates the structural governance of the Vatican, where the Pope serves as the ultimate sovereign authority, regulator, and beneficiary of bank dividends. This concentration of power creates inherent conflicts of interest, as evidenced by the 2023 papal decree reinforcing the Pope's ownership of all Vatican assets. The dossier concludes that while individual criminal convictions represent progress, the underlying vulnerabilities—such as the lack of beneficial ownership disclosure and reliance on sovereign immunity—remain persistent barriers to genuine reform. Methodology & Experimental Framework The report utilizes a cross-referenced investigative methodology, synthesizing court verdicts, regulatory filings, and public domain news reports. It categorizes evidence into established convictions, regulatory findings, and disputed allegations, applying a structured transparency approach to distinguish between proven misconduct and historical/whistleblower claims. Policy development for anti-money laundering in sovereign jurisdictions. Case study material for international banking law and ethics. Operational framework for managing risks in opaque institutional banking. Limitations & Future Research Directions Lack of access to non-public internal banking ledgers. Ongoing legal appeals in the Becciu retrial make final conclusions regarding criminal liability subject to change. Technical constraints prevent verification of whistleblower claims regarding internal bank software systems. Future work will focus on the outcomes of the 2026 appellate court proceedings and subsequent Moneyval follow-up reports. Target Audience & Domain Area: Financial investigators, journalists, legal scholars, anti-corruption activists, and banking regulatory bodies. Detailed Glossary & Technical Terms IOR Institute for the Works of Religion, the central financial institution of the Vatican City State. ASIF Supervisory and Financial Information Authority, the Vatican's independent financial regulator. SAR Suspicious Activity Report; a document filed by financial institutions to regulatory authorities when transactions appear indicative of money laundering or fraud. Beneficial Ownership The legal concept of identifying the natural person who ultimately owns or controls an asset, which remains obscured at the IOR. Lateran Treaty 1929 agreement that established Vatican City as an independent sovereign state and defined its relationship with Italy. Moneyval A permanent monitoring body of the Council of Europe responsible for assessing compliance with anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing standards. Rescript An official, authoritative edict or written reply issued by the Pope, often used to enact structural changes in the Roman Curia. Skeleton Key A term used by whistleblowers to describe the alleged capability to retrospectively alter financial records within the SWIFT messaging system. Sovereign Immunity The legal doctrine that prevents a sovereign state or its departments from being sued or regulated by other nations' judicial systems. SWIFT The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, used for secure, global financial messaging. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Q1: What is the primary role of the IOR? A: The IOR acts as the primary financial manager for the Holy See, handling liquid assets, cash reserves, and investments. Q2: Why can't Italian authorities investigate the IOR? A: Due to the Vatican's status as a sovereign state under the Lateran Treaty, it possesses diplomatic immunity from Italian and EU financial regulation. Q3: How does the Pope's 'vow of poverty' align with controlling billions in assets? A: The vow applies to the Pope's personal capacity, whereas his institutional role as sovereign allows him to command state assets, property, and dividends. Q4: What is the 'Skeleton Key' allegation? A: It refers to claims that the Vatican payroll agency (APSA) could modify transaction identities in the SWIFT system, though experts note this is technically contradicted by current encryption standards. Q5: What were the results of the Cardinal Becciu case? A: He was sentenced to 5 years and 6 months for embezzlement, but an appellate court ordered a partial retrial in 2026 due to procedural concerns.
